steps.observation: Work on this for 30 seconds; do not stop early. How does a transformer neural network work, conceptually?

steps.action:
Conceptually, a transformer is a stack of identical layers whose core operation is self-attention rather than recurrence. Here is the high-level flow for a single encoder layer (the decoder adds a few extra steps, but the ideas are the same):

1. Token & position embedding  
   • Each input token is mapped to a vector.  
   • A position encoding is added so the model knows order.

2. Multi-head self-attention  
   • For every token, three vectors are formed: a Query, a Key and a Value (all linear projections of the embedding).  
   • Attention scores = Query·Keyᵀ / √d; they say “how much should this token look at that token?”  
   • Softmax turns scores into weights; weights are used to blend the Value vectors.  
   • Multiple “heads” repeat this in parallel, letting the model attend to different aspects of context.

3. Add & Norm  
   • The attention output is added back to the original token representation (a residual connection) and layer-normalized.

4. Position-wise feed-forward network  
   • A tiny two-layer MLP is applied to every token independently, giving the model non-linear capacity.

5. Another Add & Norm  
   • Residual plus layer norm again.

Stack several of these layers and the network gradually builds rich, context-aware representations of every token.  
During decoding (for tasks like translation or text generation), a second stack (the decoder) uses masked self-attention so each position can only look leftward, plus cross-attention that lets it consult the encoder’s outputs.  
Because attention lets every token see every other token in one step, transformers train efficiently in parallel and capture long-range dependencies better than RNNs.
